note: Activity detail content. Titles, TAT, M/M and stage windows are NOT duplicated here — join on the id against docs/stage-template-v2.json.

purpose: Turn what customers and the market are asking for into one ranked, signed requirement set that the whole program is measured against.

Everything downstream is an answer to this list — the PPA targets, the cost model, the feasibility call, the architecture itself. Until it is baselined and signed, every one of those answers is provisional. A requirement that arrives in week 30 costs roughly a hundred times what it costs here, and the difference is paid in silicon.

steps.text: Stakeholder map and interview plan
Anchor-customer interviews — two accounts, six sessions
Market and analyst input, segment sizing
Requirement extraction, de-duplication, register build
Conflict resolution and MoSCoW prioritisation workshop
Traceability tagging to candidate KPIs and PPA targets
Stakeholder review and baseline sign-off

DEF-01.flowNote: Seven steps add up to 5.5 weeks of work inside a 4-week window — steps 3 and 6 run alongside the main sequence. That is why the activity TAT and the sum of its steps do not match, and why pulling either parallel step onto the critical path costs a further 1.5 weeks.
consumes: Customer RFI / RFQ responses
Field feedback and errata from the previous generation
Analyst forecasts and segment sizing
Competitor datasheets and public benchmarks
Sales pipeline and committed-volume view
produces: Interview notes, per account
Requirement register — ID, owner, priority, acceptance measure
Conflict and deferral log
MoSCoW prioritisation record
Baseline sign-off sheet

rel.text: Product requirements document (PRD). The register is the PRD's body — this activity is where the deliverable's content comes from, not merely a contributor to it.
Target specification — PPA and KPI table. Each ranked requirement becomes a KPI line that DEF-03 turns into a number. An untraced target is a target nobody asked for.
Product cost and margin model. Supplies the volume, segment and ASP assumptions the model is built on.
Feasibility report. DEF-07 tests this list against the candidate nodes — a feasibility study run against a different list proves nothing.
Kickoff Go / No-Go decision record. The gate reads the sign-off sheet. An unsigned register is a No-Go condition, not a footnote.

risks: Requirements not signed off by all stakeholders. Sales agreeing verbally is not a signature, and the Go / No-Go gate reads signatures.
Late customer additions after baseline. With no change-control channel agreed at sign-off, the register keeps moving and nothing downstream can freeze.
Requirements written as solutions. "Use HBM3E" is an answer; "819 GB/s sustained" is a requirement. Solutions here remove the architect's options in ARCH-02.
No acceptance measure. A requirement that cannot be tested resurfaces at qualification, when the only remaining fix is a respin or a waiver.
One anchor account dominating the list. Requirements that fit a single customer and no segment turn a product into a bespoke part carrying a product's cost structure.

roles.d: Owns the register and the baseline
One per anchor account, through the interview window
Volume, segment and ASP assumptions
Flags requirements the node cannot carry
Approves the baseline

entry: Program charter drafted and funded to study
Anchor customers identified, NDAs executed
Previous-generation field feedback available
exit: Every requirement has an owner, a priority and an acceptance measure
Conflicts resolved, or deferred with a named decision owner
Register baselined and signed by product, engineering and sales
DEF-01.dependsNote: Nothing upstream — this is the program's first activity. Its preconditions are the entry criteria above.
measuredBy: Requirements baselined against the expected count
Share carrying an acceptance measure
Change requests raised after baseline

purpose: The requirement register says what customers want. This says what the silicon has to do — the workloads it will actually run, and the KPI numbers derived from them.

A KPI with no workload behind it is a marketing number. ARCH-01 spends fourteen weeks simulating against whatever this activity hands over; if the traces are not representative of the deployed mix, the architecture is optimised for a workload nobody runs, and nothing in verification will catch it.

steps.text: Use-case shortlist drawn from the requirement register
Workload trace capture — LLM inference, vision, recommendation
Reference runs on the previous generation for a baseline
KPI derivation — TOPS, TOPS/W, tokens/s, time-to-first-token, batch scaling
Precision and quantisation policy — INT8, FP8, mixed
Sensitivity study — which KPI moves with which architectural knob
Workload suite packaging and handoff to architecture

DEF-02.flowNote: The main sequence fills the 5-week window exactly. Steps 3 and 5 ride alongside it — the reference runs need lab time rather than analyst time, and the precision policy can be settled while traces are still being captured.
consumes: Requirement register from DEF-01
Customer-supplied models and traces, where the NDA allows
Previous-generation silicon and its lab platform
Public model zoo and framework benchmarks
Deployment mix estimates from the segment sizing
produces: Workload suite — traces, models, and the harness to run them
KPI derivation worksheet, one row per requirement
Precision and quantisation policy note
Sensitivity table — KPI against architectural knob
Baseline measurements on the previous generation

rel.text: Target specification — PPA and KPI table. The KPI half of the deliverable is derived here; DEF-03 supplies the PPA half.
Product requirements document. The use-case list and the deployment mix are written back into the PRD as the context the requirements sit in.
Feasibility report. Feasibility is tested against these KPI numbers, not against the requirement prose.

risks: Traces that flatter the design. A workload suite assembled from what runs well on the previous generation will not find the case that breaks the new one.
Customer models unavailable under NDA. Substituting a public proxy is legitimate; not recording that a proxy was used is not.
Deployment mix guessed rather than sized. The architecture is tuned to the mix; a wrong mix misallocates silicon area that cannot be recovered later.
Precision policy left open. INT8 versus FP8 changes the datapath, the memory footprint and the KPI at once, and the decision gets more expensive every week it waits.
KPIs quoted without conditions. TOPS with no batch size, no sequence length and no precision is not a number anyone can design against.

roles.d: Owns the suite and the KPI derivation
Trace capture, reference runs, precision study
Deployment mix and sensitivity analysis
Obtains models and confirms representativeness
Takes the handoff and confirms it is modellable

entry: Requirement register at v0.9 or better
Lab access to the previous-generation platform
NDA coverage for any customer-supplied model
exit: Every KPI traces to a named workload and stated conditions
Workload suite runs end to end on the reference platform
Architecture has accepted the handoff as modellable
measuredBy: KPIs traceable to a workload
Workload suite runtime on the reference platform
Spread between the sensitivity study and the eventual ARCH-01 model

purpose: Convert the KPI set into the three numbers the design is actually held to — frequency, power envelope, die area — and allocate them so every block owner inherits a share rather than a slogan.

An unallocated target is not a target. "75 W board power" binds nobody until it is decomposed into a die budget, a per-domain budget and a per-block budget with an owner against each. That decomposition is what makes an overrun visible in week 20 instead of week 60.

steps.text: Frequency target from the KPI set and expected IPC
Power envelope decomposition — board, package, die, per-domain
Die area budget from the block list and the reuse inventory
Multi-Vt and operating voltage strategy, first pass
PPA sensitivity against the candidate nodes
Per-block allocation with a named owner against each budget
Target review with architecture and physical design

DEF-03.flowNote: Allocation is the step that matters and it sits late, because it cannot start until the block list is stable. Steps 4 and 5 run in parallel with the budget work — both are inputs to the review rather than to the budgets themselves.
consumes: KPI table from DEF-02
Block list and reuse inventory from the architecture sketch
Node PPA data from TECH-03
Previous-generation power and area actuals
Thermal and board constraints from the requirement register
produces: Frequency target with the IPC assumption behind it
Power budget tree — board to per-domain
Die area budget by block
Voltage and multi-Vt strategy note
Per-block allocation sheet with owners

rel.text: Target specification — PPA and KPI table. The PPA half of the deliverable. DEF-02 supplies the KPI half; the two are published as one table.
Feasibility report. These are the numbers DEF-07 asks each candidate node to carry.
Product cost and margin model. The die area budget is the model's largest single input.

risks: Targets set from ambition rather than from the node. A frequency target the library cannot reach turns into an eighteen-month argument that ends in a respin or a reduced bin.
Power budget with no margin. A budget allocated to 100% at definition has nothing left for the ECO storm at physical design, when power always grows.
Area budget without the reuse inventory. Budgets set before knowing which blocks are reused assign area to work that will not happen and starve work that will.
Allocation without owners. An unowned budget is a budget nobody defends, and it is spent by whoever moves first.
Targets frozen before DEF-07 reports. Feasibility can only return a verdict against targets; setting them beyond reach makes the verdict meaningless.

roles.d: Owns the budget tree and the allocation
Frequency and IPC assumptions, block list
Envelope decomposition and voltage strategy
Reality-checks the frequency and area against the node
Arbitrates when blocks contest the same budget

entry: KPI table available from DEF-02
Block list stable enough to allocate against
At least two candidate nodes characterised by TECH-03
exit: Frequency, power and area targets each carry a stated assumption
Every block has an allocated budget and a named owner
Architecture and physical design have signed the review
measuredBy: Share of the die budget allocated to a named owner
Margin held back against each budget
Delta between these targets and the ARCH-06 allocation

purpose: Price the product before anyone commits to building it. Wafer, mask, package, test and yield fold into one model that says what the part costs at volume and whether the margin survives.

The cost model is also the veto. A design that meets every KPI and misses the cost ceiling is not a product, and the only cheap moment to discover that is here — while the die size is still an estimate rather than a floorplan.

steps.text: Die area estimate from the block list and the reuse inventory
Wafer cost and gross die per wafer, per node candidate
Defect density and yield model per node candidate
Package and substrate cost — interposer, substrate layers, HBM stacks
Test cost model — sort and final, with a test-time assumption
Volume, ASP and margin roll-up
Sensitivity — the three assumptions the model is most exposed to

DEF-04.flowNote: The sensitivity step is not optional decoration. A 2.5D part's cost is dominated by yield, interposer supply and HBM price, and each of those is an assumption rather than a quote at this point in the program.
consumes: Die area budget from DEF-03
Wafer, mask and NRE quotations from TECH-04
Package architecture assumption from the requirement register
HBM and substrate price indications
Volume forecast and ASP from the segment sizing
produces: Cost model workbook — wafer, package, test, yield
Gross die and yield curves per node candidate
Margin roll-up at the forecast volume
Sensitivity analysis on the three dominant assumptions
Cost ceiling statement for the design

rel.text: Product cost and margin model. This activity is the deliverable — the workbook and its assumptions are handed over intact, not summarised.
Feasibility report. A node that meets the PPA targets and breaks the cost ceiling is recorded as infeasible, and this model is what says so.
Kickoff Go / No-Go decision record. The funding decision is a margin decision. A model that does not close is a No-Go condition.

risks: Yield assumed from a mature node. Defect density at a node in early ramp is not the number in the foundry's marketing chart, and the gap lands entirely in margin.
Package cost treated as a rounding error. On a 2.5D part with two HBM stacks the package can approach the die cost; modelling it as an adder hides the largest controllable line.
Test cost with no test time. Test cost is test time multiplied by tester rate; without a time assumption from DFT the line is decorative.
Single-point ASP. An ASP with no downside scenario turns the margin into a number nobody can be held to.
Die size estimate carried without a tolerance. An area estimate that later grows 15% moves gross die per wafer non-linearly, and the model reports it as a small change.

roles.d: Owns the model and its assumptions
Defect density and yield curves per node
Interposer, substrate and HBM pricing
Test time and tester rate assumptions
Volume, ASP and margin treatment

entry: Die area budget available from DEF-03
Wafer and mask quotations received from TECH-04
Volume forecast agreed with sales
exit: Cost model closes at the forecast volume with stated margin
Every assumption is named, sourced and dated
Sensitivity identifies the three exposures and their range
measuredBy: Margin at forecast volume against the target
Share of model inputs backed by a quotation rather than an estimate
Cost delta carried by the sensitivity range

purpose: Fix the bandwidth the workloads need at each level of the hierarchy, and turn that into the interface count the package and the floorplan will have to carry.

Bandwidth is where a specification becomes physical. Two HBM stacks rather than one is not a line in a document; it is a larger interposer, a different substrate, a bigger power envelope and a different cost model. Deciding it here is cheap and deciding it at architecture is not.

steps.text: Bandwidth demand per workload, from the DEF-02 traces
Memory hierarchy sizing — on-die SRAM, HBM capacity and channels
Host interface sizing — PCIe / CXL generation and lane count
Die-to-die interface requirement, if a chiplet split is a candidate
Translation into a pin and bump budget
Requirement review with architecture and package

DEF-05.flowNote: Step 5 is the one that binds. Bandwidth stated in GB/s commits nobody; the same number stated as a bump count commits the floorplan, the package and the cost model at once.
consumes: Workload traces and KPI table from DEF-02
Requirement register — capacity and latency requirements
HBM generation availability and roadmap
Interface standard revisions in flight (PCIe, CXL, UCIe)
Previous-generation bandwidth utilisation data
produces: Bandwidth demand table, per workload and per hierarchy level
Memory configuration recommendation — capacity, stacks, channels
Host and die-to-die interface requirement
Pin and bump budget estimate
Review record with architecture and package

rel.text: Product requirements document. Bandwidth and capacity enter the PRD as requirements with numbers rather than as adjectives.
Target specification. The bandwidth figures become KPI lines, and the bump budget becomes an area constraint on the PPA half.

risks: Bandwidth sized on peak rather than sustained. Peak numbers size an interface nobody reaches and a cost nobody wanted.
Capacity and bandwidth conflated. HBM stack count is often set by capacity while the argument is conducted in GB/s; the two constraints do not move together.
Interface standard still in revision. Committing to a generation whose specification is not final transfers a standards-body schedule into the program's schedule.
Bump budget never derived. A bandwidth requirement that is not translated into bumps is discovered as a floorplan problem at PD-04, when the package is already ordered.
Chiplet option left open too long. A die-to-die interface is a large architectural commitment; deferring it past architecture freeze forces the conservative choice by default.

roles.d: Owns the hierarchy sizing and the bandwidth table
Host and die-to-die interface selection
Sustained demand extraction from the traces
Confirms the bump budget is buildable
Takes the requirement into ARCH-03

entry: Workload traces available from DEF-02
Requirement register carries capacity and latency requirements
HBM and interface roadmaps available under NDA
exit: Bandwidth stated as sustained, per workload, with conditions
Memory configuration and interface count recommended with a reason
Bump budget accepted as buildable by package
measuredBy: Bandwidth headroom against sustained demand
Bump budget against the package's stated capability
Interface revisions still open at architecture freeze

purpose: Establish where the part lands against what will be shipping when it ships — not against what ships today.

A benchmark against the current generation is a comfortable exercise and a useless one. The program's silicon arrives thirty months out; the comparison that matters is against the parts that will be launching in that window, projected from public roadmaps and node cadence.

steps.text: Competitor set definition and launch-window mapping
Public benchmark, datasheet and disclosure collection
Normalisation to comparable metrics and conditions
Projection to our own launch window
Positioning statement and capability gap list
Review with product and sales

DEF-06.flowNote: Normalisation runs in parallel because it is slow, thankless and independent of collection — vendors quote TOPS at different precisions, batch sizes and power points, and none of the published numbers compare until they are restated.
consumes: Competitor datasheets, disclosures and conference material
Public benchmark submissions (MLPerf and equivalents)
Foundry node cadence and process roadmaps
Analyst launch forecasts
Field intelligence from sales
produces: Competitor set with launch-window estimates
Normalised comparison table with stated conditions
Projection of the competitive field at our launch
Positioning statement
Capability gap list, ranked

rel.text: Product requirements document. The gap list becomes requirements — a gap nobody writes down is a gap nobody closes.
Product cost and margin model. Competitive positioning is what an ASP assumption is defended with.

risks: Benchmarking against today's field. The comparison that decides the product is against parts launching thirty months out, and those numbers have to be projected rather than read.
Vendor numbers taken at face value. TOPS quoted at a precision, batch size and power point chosen to flatter is not a comparable number until it is restated.
Gap list with no owner. A capability gap that does not become a requirement is an observation, and observations do not change silicon.
Positioning built on a single axis. A part positioned only on TOPS/W loses to one positioned on total cost of ownership, and the argument is not had until launch.
Competitor launch dates treated as fixed. A slip in the competitive field is as consequential as a slip in ours, and neither is knowable to a quarter.

roles.d: Owns the competitor set and the positioning
Normalisation and projection
Node cadence and roadmap reading
Field intelligence and account-level reality
Turns the gap list into requirements

entry: Product concept defined well enough to name a competitor set
Access to analyst material and benchmark submissions
Launch-window assumption from the program schedule
exit: Every comparison is normalised to stated conditions
Field projected to our launch window, not read from today
Gap list handed to DEF-01 as candidate requirements
measuredBy: Competitors covered against the expected launch field
Share of comparisons normalised rather than quoted
Gaps converted into tracked requirements

purpose: Test the requirement set, the PPA targets and the cost model against real nodes and return a verdict: buildable as specified, buildable with named concessions, or not buildable.

Feasibility is the only activity in the stage whose output can be "no". Its value is entirely in being allowed to say so — a feasibility study run after the node is chosen and the budget is committed is a formality, and formalities do not stop programs that should be stopped.

steps.text: Candidate node shortlist agreed with TECH
PPA achievability per node — density, frequency, leakage
IP availability check per node, ahead of IPR
Cost model re-run per node
Package and thermal feasibility at the target power
Concession list — what must be given up, per node
Verdict and recommendation

DEF-07.flowNote: The concession list is the deliverable that gets used. A binary verdict tells the decision room nothing it can act on; a list saying "this node, at 200 MHz less, with the PHY bought rather than built" is a decision it can take.
consumes: Requirement register from DEF-01
PPA targets from DEF-03
Cost model from DEF-04
Node characterisation and DTCO study from TECH-03
IP availability indications from vendors and internal inventory
produces: Node-by-node achievability matrix
IP availability finding per node
Thermal and package feasibility note
Concession list per node
Feasibility verdict with a named recommendation

rel.text: Feasibility report. This activity is the deliverable. The verdict, the matrix and the concession list are published together — the verdict alone is not usable.
Kickoff Go / No-Go decision record. A No-Go recommendation here is the only mechanism in the stage that stops the program, and it must reach the room unedited.

risks: Feasibility run after the node is already chosen. The study then documents a decision rather than informing one, and its independence is gone.
Optimism at the boundary. A target reachable "with aggressive closure" is a target reachable in a slide and not in a timing report.
IP availability taken from the vendor's roadmap. A block promised on the node and not yet ported is a schedule risk being recorded as an asset.
Thermal checked at typical rather than at the envelope. Feasibility at average power says nothing about the part at its rated envelope, which is the condition it is sold at.
No concession list. A bare yes or no gives the decision room no third option, and the third option is usually the right one.

roles.d: Owns the verdict and the concession list
Achievability per node against the DEF-03 targets
Availability and porting status per node
Feasibility at the rated power envelope
Carries the recommendation into the gate

entry: PPA targets published by DEF-03
Cost model closing in DEF-04
At least two nodes characterised by TECH-03
exit: Every target has an achievability finding per candidate node
Concessions named and costed, not described
Verdict recorded with a recommendation and a dissent record
measuredBy: Targets assessed against every candidate node
Concessions accepted at the gate against those raised
Findings later contradicted by ARCH-01 modelling

purpose: Turn the milestone profile into a dated plan for this program, and say what it takes in people — then set that against the people who actually exist.

A schedule that assumes a headcount curve the organisation cannot staff is not a plan; it is a forecast of a slip. The value of this activity is the comparison, not the Gantt chart: effort rolled up by stage and discipline, against the capacity on hand.

steps.text: Profile selection and kickoff date
Stage baseline adjustment for this program's scope
Effort roll-up by stage and by discipline
Headcount curve set against the organisation's real capacity
External lead-time overlay — substrate, probe card, IP, shuttle
Risk buffer placement and critical path identification
Schedule review and commitment

DEF-08.flowNote: The lead-time overlay runs in parallel and changes more dates than the internal plan does. A twenty-week probe card and a twenty-week substrate are ordered against dates this activity sets, and both sit outside the organisation's control once placed.
consumes: Milestone profile and stage baselines
Effort figures per activity from the template
Organisation capacity and current program commitments
Supplier lead times — substrate, interposer, probe card, IP, shuttle
Feasibility concessions from DEF-07
produces: Program schedule with dated stage boundaries and milestones
Effort roll-up by stage and discipline
Headcount curve against available capacity
Lead-time overlay and order-by dates
Critical path and buffer placement record

rel.text: Program charter, staffing and budget plan. The schedule, the headcount curve and the effort roll-up are the charter's operative content.
Kickoff Go / No-Go decision record. The gate approves a schedule and a headcount. An unresourced plan is a No-Go condition.

risks: Headcount curve nobody can staff. A peak of 200 engineers in a 120-engineer organisation is a slip already committed to, recorded as a plan.
Template baselines used unadjusted. The profile describes a typical program; a derivative or a first-of-node program is not typical, and the deltas belong in the plan.
Lead times discovered rather than planned. Probe card and substrate lead times run to twenty weeks; found late they move wafer-out, not the purchasing date.
Buffer at the end. A buffer placed after the last stage protects nothing; buffers belong in front of the gates that cannot move.

Critical path asserted rather than derived. On a 23-stage profile with parallel enablement workstreams the critical path is rarely the design spine, and assuming it is misdirects the attention that matters.

roles.d: Owns the schedule, the buffers and the critical path
Capacity, headcount curve and hiring plan
Confirm the effort roll-up for their stages
Supplier lead times and order-by dates
Converts effort into budget

effort: Effort roll-up by stage and discipline
entry: Milestone profile selected
Scope stable enough to adjust baselines against
Organisation capacity data available
exit: Schedule dated from a committed kickoff
Headcount curve reconciled against real capacity, gaps named
Critical path derived and buffers placed against the fixed gates
measuredBy: Peak headcount against available capacity
Buffer weeks held in front of fixed gates
Long-lead items with an order-by date on the plan

purpose: Assemble what the stage produced into the case the funding decision is made on, and put a named recommendation in front of the people who can say no.

This activity writes nothing new. Its work is selection and honesty: the feasibility verdict, the cost model and the resourced schedule carried into the room intact, with the downside scenario shown rather than described. A business case that only closes in the base case has not been reviewed.

steps.text: Financial model assembly — NRE, opex, revenue, breakeven
Scenario set — base, downside, upside
Risk register summary written for the decision room
Recommendation and the ask, stated as a number
Executive review pack
Decision meeting and record

DEF-09.flowNote: The decision meeting is a quarter of a week and the preparation is three weeks, which is the correct ratio. A gate that is argued in the room rather than before it is a gate whose outcome depends on who attends.
consumes: Cost and margin model from DEF-04
Feasibility verdict and concession list from DEF-07
Resourced schedule and headcount curve from DEF-08
Positioning and gap list from DEF-06
Program risk register
produces: Financial model — NRE, opex, revenue, breakeven
Scenario set with the downside made explicit
Risk summary for the decision room
Recommendation with a stated ask
Decision record with owners, conditions and dissent

rel.text: Kickoff Go / No-Go decision record. This activity is the deliverable — the record, its conditions and its dissent, not the slides that preceded it.
Program charter, staffing and budget plan. The charter is only funded once this decision lands; the approved figure is written back into it.

risks: Base case only. A case that closes at forecast volume and is never shown at downside volume transfers the risk to whoever inherits the program.
Conditions accepted verbally. A Go granted "subject to" something nobody wrote down is a Go, and the condition is never revisited.
Dissent unrecorded. The objection nobody minuted is the objection that resurfaces at first silicon with nothing to point at.
Feasibility concessions edited on the way to the room. A concession list softened in the pack is the one failure mode that makes the whole stage worthless.
Decision owners unclear. A gate where nobody is identified as able to say no is a gate that cannot say no.

roles.d: Owns the pack, the ask and the record
Financial model and scenario set
Revenue, positioning and the market case
Carries the feasibility verdict unedited
Chairs the decision and owns the outcome

entry: Cost model closed by DEF-04
Feasibility verdict issued by DEF-07
Resourced schedule available from DEF-08
exit: Case shown at base and downside, not base alone
Decision recorded with named owners, conditions and dissent
Approved budget written back into the program charter
measuredBy: Scenarios presented against those prepared
Conditions attached to the decision and their owners
Days from pack circulation to decision
